title: Google TPU Sync: Open-Source KV Cache Transfer Library
summary: Google released TPU Sync, an open-source C++ library that reduces KV cache transfer latency by over 90% on 235B to 480B parameter MoE models.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Google officially released TPU Sync, an open-source C++ library for transferring KV caches and weights across TPU memory tiers.
- The library achieves over 90% lower transfer latency on models ranging from 235 billion to 480 billion parameters.
- TPU Sync supports transfers across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and network, enabling efficient large-scale inference workflows.


Google has officially launched TPU Sync, an open-source C++ library designed to streamline the transfer of[KV caches](https://emergent.sh/glossary/kv-cache) and model weights across TPU memory hierarchies. Officially released on November 13, 2026, the library targets large-scale inference workloads, particularly mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures ranging from 235 billion to 480 billion parameters. According to Google, TPU Sync reduces transfer latency by over 90% compared to existing approaches, marking a significant infrastructure gain for enterprises deploying massive language models on TPU hardware.


## What TPU Sync Does


TPU Sync handles the movement of key-value caches and model weights between four memory tiers: TPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), host DRAM, persistent storage, and network-attached resources. The library abstracts low-level memory management, enabling developers to orchestrate data flows without writing custom DMA logic or dealing with TPU-specific APIs. This is critical for MoE models, where active experts must be swapped in and out of HBM rapidly during inference. By automating these transfers, TPU Sync cuts idle time and improves token throughput on multi-chip TPU pods.


## Performance Gains on MoE Models


Google tested the library on models between 235 billion and 480 billion parameters, all using mixture-of-experts architectures. In these benchmarks, TPU Sync achieved over 90% lower latency for KV cache transfers compared to baseline methods that relied on host-side copying or manual staging. For a 480 billion parameter model, this translates to several milliseconds saved per forward pass, compounding across thousands of requests per second. The gains are especially pronounced in batch inference scenarios, where cache reuse and prefetching strategies are coordinated by the library's scheduler.


## Open Source Availability


The library is distributed under an open-source license, with full source code and build scripts available on GitHub. Google has released documentation covering API usage, integration with JAX and TensorFlow serving pipelines, and tuning parameters for different TPU topologies. Early adopters can compile TPU Sync into existing inference stacks with minimal refactoring, though optimal performance requires alignment with Google's recommended pod configurations and software versions. Community contributions are encouraged, particularly for extending support to non-MoE architectures and cross-cloud memory fabrics.


## Release Date and Roadmap


TPU Sync was officially released on November 13, 2026. Google indicated that future updates will focus on multi-tenancy features, allowing isolated cache pools for concurrent workloads, and integration with the broader TPU software stack, including profiling tools and automatic tuning heuristics. The company also hinted at extending support for sparse attention patterns and disaggregated serving topologies, where model weights reside on remote storage tiers and are fetched on demand.


## What This Means


TPU Sync lowers the operational complexity and cost of running ultra-large MoE models on TPU infrastructure. By open sourcing the library, Google enables research labs and enterprises to achieve near-optimal memory bandwidth utilization without proprietary tooling. For organizations already invested in TPU hardware, this release removes a major bottleneck in scaling inference to hundreds of billions of parameters. It also positions Google's TPU ecosystem as a more competitive alternative to GPU-based stacks, where similar cache management optimizations have historically required vendor-specific libraries or custom CUDA kernels.
